body:
Why local time differs from place to place

The Earth rotates on its axis from west to east. As a result, the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west. Places farther east generally experience the successive stages of the Sun's apparent daily movement before places farther west.

At a particular moment, one meridian may face the Sun directly, another may be experiencing sunrise, and another may be in darkness. This difference in the position of the Sun provides the geographical basis for local time.

Local solar time

Local solar time is time determined by the apparent daily movement of the Sun at a particular longitude.

Local solar noon occurs when the Sun crosses the local meridian and reaches its highest daily position in the sky at an ordinary non-polar location. A vertical object's shadow is generally shortest at this time.

The Sun need not be directly overhead for solar noon to occur. For most places, the Sun reaches its highest daily position without becoming vertical.

Actual apparent solar time varies slightly over the year. Geographical time calculations normally use local mean solar time, based on the average solar day of 24 hours.

The relationship between longitude and time

During an average solar day, the Earth's daily rotation relative to the Sun corresponds to 360° of longitude over 24 hours. Therefore:

$$\frac{360^\circ}{24\text{ hours}}=15^\circ\text{ per hour}$$

The corresponding time difference for 1° of longitude is:

$$\frac{60\text{ minutes}}{15}=4\text{ minutes}$$

These relationships allow the difference in local mean solar time between places to be calculated from their longitudes.

Longitude differenceTime difference
1′ of longitude4 seconds
15′ of longitude1 minute
1°4 minutes
7°30′30 minutes
15°1 hour
90°6 hours
180°12 hours
360°24 hours

Minutes of arc and minutes of time are different units. For example, 30′ of longitude represents half a degree and therefore corresponds to 2 minutes of time.

Eastward and westward time differences

Relative to a reference meridian, local time is generally ahead towards the east and behind towards the west. This rule applies to ordinary longitude-time calculations, with a separate calendar-date adjustment when crossing the International Date Line.

Moving eastward increases local time. Moving westward decreases local time.

Suppose the local time at Greenwich, 0° longitude, is 12:00 noon:

  • At 30°W, local time is 10:00.
  • At 15°W, local time is 11:00.
  • At 15°E, local time is 13:00.
  • At 30°E, local time is 14:00.

Does latitude affect local time?

Places located on the same meridian have the same local mean solar time, even when their latitudes differ considerably.

For instance, hypothetical locations at 10°N, 75°E and 40°N, 75°E have the same local mean solar time because their longitude is identical. However, their sunrise times, sunset times and seasonal durations of daylight can differ because their latitudes are different.

Conversely, places situated on the same parallel but on different meridians generally have different local mean solar times.

Prelims focus

  • The Earth rotates from west to east.
  • 15° of longitude corresponds to 1 hour of local time.
  • 1° of longitude corresponds to 4 minutes of local time.
  • Eastward locations are ahead; westward locations are behind.
  • Places on the same meridian have the same local mean solar time.
  • Trap: Equal local solar time does not necessarily mean equal sunrise or sunset time.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 14–16; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Standard 6, Chapter 1, pp. 15–21; Royal Museums Greenwich, What is Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) – and why does it matter?, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: At one instant, local time rises from 10:00 at 30°W to 14:00 at 30°E. Moving east adds time; moving west subtracts time.
pictures.caption: Longitude determines the difference in local mean solar time.

title: Earth's Rotation, Longitude and Local Time

body:
Why standard time is necessary

If every town maintained a clock based on its own local solar time, places separated by even a few degrees of longitude would have different clock readings. Railway schedules, communication, administrative work and commercial activities would become difficult to coordinate.

For this reason, countries and territories adopt common official times for particular geographical areas.

Standard time is the uniform official time adopted for a country, territory or time zone, irrespective of the different local solar times within that area.

In the traditional geographical system, a suitable reference longitude is selected as the standard meridian. Its local mean solar time provides the basis for the area's standard time.

Greenwich Mean Time

Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) originated as mean solar time at the Greenwich meridian. Greenwich was internationally selected as the reference for measuring longitude in 1884.

GMT became an important reference for comparing local times and standard times around the world. A standard time expressed as GMT+3 is 3 hours ahead of GMT, while GMT−5 is 5 hours behind GMT.

Coordinated Universal Time

Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the modern international time reference used for civil timekeeping. It is maintained using highly precise atomic time standards.

UTC replaced GMT as the international civil time standard in 1972. For ordinary geographical calculations involving hours and minutes, GMT and UTC can generally be treated as equivalent reference times. They nevertheless have different technical definitions.

UTC itself does not change according to seasonal clock adjustments.

GMT is historically based on mean solar time at Greenwich. UTC is the modern international reference for standard clock time.

The ideal system of 24 time zones

A time zone is a geographical region within which a common standard time is observed.

The conventional geographical division of the Earth into time zones is based on its 360° rotation during a 24-hour day. In the ideal system, there are 24 time zones, each extending across 15° of longitude.

The reference meridians are separated by 15° and have a difference of 1 hour in local mean solar time. An ideal time zone extends approximately 7°30′ on either side of its central meridian.

For example, the ideal time zone centred on 15°E extends from 7°30′E to 22°30′E. Its standard time would be 1 hour ahead of Greenwich.

Why actual time zones are irregular

Actual time-zone boundaries do not consistently follow straight meridians. Countries adjust their official times and territorial time-zone boundaries to suit administrative, economic and social needs.

  • A country with a considerable east-west extent may adopt several time zones. Russia, Canada and the United States are examples.
  • A country may adopt a single national standard time despite substantial differences in local solar time. India follows this approach.
  • Official time offsets are not necessarily whole numbers of hours. India, for example, observes UTC+05:30.
  • Some countries or regions seasonally advance their clocks under daylight saving time arrangements.

Consequently, the ideal model of 24 equal zones should not be confused with the actual worldwide arrangement of official time zones and UTC offsets.

Local time and standard time compared

FeatureLocal mean solar timeStandard time
BasisLongitude of the placeAdopted official time reference
VariationVaries with longitudeUniform within a time zone
Calculation4 minutes per degreeOfficial UTC offset
Primary significancePosition of the mean SunCommon civil clock time

Two places can have different longitudes and local solar times but identical official clock times if they belong to the same time zone.

Prelims focus

  • Standard time provides a common official clock time.
  • GMT originated from mean solar time at Greenwich.
  • UTC is the modern international time reference.
  • The ideal system has 24 time zones of 15° each.
  • Actual time-zone boundaries frequently follow administrative or political considerations.
  • Trap: All actual time zones are not necessarily 15° wide or separated by whole-hour offsets.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 15–16; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Standard 6, Chapter 1, pp. 20–24; Royal Museums Greenwich, What is Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) – and why does it matter?; NOAA, Z-time (Coordinated Universal Time), consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Greenwich Mean Time, UTC and World Time Zones

body:
The standard meridian of India

India has a considerable longitudinal extent. The differences in local solar time between its eastern and western regions make it necessary to use a common national clock time.

The longitude selected as the standard meridian of India is 82°30′E. It passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.

The local mean solar time corresponding to this meridian provides the geographical basis of Indian Standard Time (IST).

Calculating IST from Greenwich time

The standard meridian of India lies 82°30′ east of Greenwich. Since 30′ is half a degree, this longitude is equivalent to 82.5°E.

Each degree of longitude corresponds to 4 minutes of time.

$$82.5\times4=330\text{ minutes}$$

330 minutes is equal to 5 hours and 30 minutes. India lies east of Greenwich, so this interval is added to Greenwich time.

IST = UTC + 05:30.

Indian Standard Time is 5 hours and 30 minutes ahead of the international reference time.

For example, when the time at UTC is 12:00 noon, the corresponding IST is 17:30.

As of 26 November 2026, India continues to observe a single official national standard time of UTC+05:30. It is maintained and disseminated by the CSIR-National Physical Laboratory, India's national measurement institute. Modern IST is maintained through precise timekeeping systems rather than by observing the Sun at Mirzapur each day.

India's latitudinal and longitudinal extent

The conventional geographical coordinates of mainland India are:

  • Southern latitude: 8°4′N.
  • Northern latitude: 37°6′N.
  • Western longitude: 68°7′E.
  • Eastern longitude: 97°25′E.

These values place mainland India entirely within the Northern and Eastern Hemispheres.

The latitudinal extent of mainland India is 29°2′, while its longitudinal extent is 29°18′. Both are approximately 30°, but the ground distances corresponding to them differ because meridians converge towards the poles.

Time difference between eastern and western India

The longitudinal difference between the easternmost and westernmost reference longitudes is:

$$97^\circ25′-68^\circ7′=29^\circ18′$$

The corresponding local mean solar time difference is 116 minutes for 29° and 72 seconds for 18′. The total is 117 minutes and 12 seconds, or approximately 2 hours.

Thus, the local mean solar time at India's eastern longitudinal extreme is almost 2 hours ahead of that at its western extreme.

Important reference lines passing through India

The Tropic of Cancer

The Tropic of Cancer, conventionally represented as 23°30′N, passes through India from west to east. It crosses the following 8 states in geographical order:

  1. Gujarat
  2. Rajasthan
  3. Madhya Pradesh
  4. Chhattisgarh
  5. Jharkhand
  6. West Bengal
  7. Tripura
  8. Mizoram

The Indian Standard Meridian

The standard meridian of 82°30′E crosses the following 5 states:

  1. Uttar Pradesh
  2. Madhya Pradesh
  3. Chhattisgarh
  4. Odisha
  5. Andhra Pradesh

Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh are crossed by both these reference lines. Gujarat is crossed by the Tropic of Cancer but not by the Indian Standard Meridian.

Local solar time in Gujarat

Gujarat is situated west of India's standard meridian. Therefore, its local mean solar time is behind IST. The difference depends on the exact longitude of the location.

By contrast, places in eastern India located east of 82°30′E have local mean solar times ahead of IST.

A comparison across India

Consider a representative location in Gujarat at 72°30′E and another location in eastern India at 92°30′E.

Both are separated from the standard meridian by 10°, but on opposite sides.

When IST is 12:00, the western location has a local mean solar time of 11:20, while the eastern location has a local mean solar time of 12:40. The official clocks at both locations nevertheless show 12:00 IST.

This explains why sunrise and sunset can occur substantially earlier by the official clock in northeastern India than in Gujarat. The exact sunrise and sunset differences also depend on latitude and season.

Prelims focus

  • Indian Standard Meridian: 82°30′E, near Mirzapur, Uttar Pradesh.
  • IST: UTC+05:30, maintained by CSIR-National Physical Laboratory.
  • India's east-west local mean solar time difference is approximately 2 hours.
  • The Tropic of Cancer crosses 8 Indian states; the standard meridian crosses 5.
  • Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh are crossed by both reference lines.
  • Trap: Gujarat's local mean solar time is behind IST, but its official clock time is IST.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 15–16; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 3, p. 32; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 13, pp. 99–100, online textbook copy consulted 26 November 2026; Department of Education, Government of NCT of Delhi, Class 10 Social Science Support Material, NIOS Project, 2025, p. 45; CSIR-National Physical Laboratory, NPL-India Web Time Display and Time and Frequency Metrology, consulted 26 November 2026.]
